Packages: `vars`, `urca`, `yaml`, `xts` (installation: `Rscript R/install_packages.R`).

This notebook repeats the steps of `notebooks/python/04_var_vecm.ipynb` with the reference R packages, `vars` and `urca`, then compares each result with the files written by Python. The Python notebook must therefore be run **before** this one.

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
# Resolve the project root once so every path below is relative to it, whatever folder knitr runs in.
ROOT <- dirname(normalizePath(knitr::current_input(dir = TRUE), winslash = "/"))
while (!file.exists(file.path(ROOT, "config.yaml"))) ROOT <- dirname(ROOT)
source(file.path(ROOT, "R", "load_data.R"))
source(file.path(ROOT, "R", "var_helpers.R"))
knitr::opts_knit$set(root.dir = ROOT)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, comment = "", fig.width = 10, fig.height = 6)
cfg <- load_config(ROOT)
set.seed(cfg$seed)  # same seed as Python; nothing below is random
RES <- file.path(ROOT, cfg$paths$results)
fmt <- function(x) sprintf("%.2g", x)
```

## 0. Data

```{r data}
# Same CSV and same pivot as Python; returns for the VAR (I(0)), log prices for cointegration (I(1)).
panel <- load_panel(ROOT)
V <- c("BTC", "NVDA", "CONVERTS", "PURE")   # same column order = same Cholesky order as Python
ret <- na.omit(panel[, paste0(V, "_log_return")]); colnames(ret) <- V
lp <- panel[, paste0(V, "_log_price")]; colnames(lp) <- V
PER <- period_rows(ret, cfg$pivot_date)
LPER <- period_rows(lp, cfg$pivot_date)
sapply(PER, nrow)
```

## 1. VAR on returns

```{r lags}
# Information criteria for p = 1..10 (vars::VARselect starts at p = 1, unlike statsmodels which also reports p = 0).
sel <- t(sapply(PER, function(x) VARselect(zoo::coredata(x), lag.max = 10, type = "const")$selection))
sel
```

`VARselect` does not offer p = 0. Among p ≥ 1, it chooses the smallest possible order. Python, which also tests p = 0, chooses 0 with all four criteria in the three periods. The two therefore agree: no dynamics beyond one day. We estimate a **VAR(1)**, the minimum order that allows testing Granger causality.

```{r var}
# VAR(1) with a constant in each period, then stability and the three residual tests of the brief.
vars_r <- lapply(PER, function(x) VAR(zoo::coredata(x), p = 1, type = "const"))
diag_r <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(vars_r), function(n) {
  v <- vars_r[[n]]
  pt <- serial.test(v, lags.pt = 10, type = "PT.adjusted")$serial
  jb <- normality.test(v, multivariate.only = TRUE)$jb.mul$JB
  ar <- arch.test(v, lags.multi = 5, multivariate.only = TRUE)$arch.mul
  data.frame(period = n, max_root = max(roots(v)),
             portmanteau_stat = unname(pt$statistic), portmanteau_p = pt$p.value,
             JB_mult_stat = unname(jb$statistic), JB_mult_p = jb$p.value,
             ARCH_mult_stat = unname(ar$statistic), ARCH_mult_p = ar$p.value)
}))
write.csv(diag_r, file.path(RES, "04_var_diagnostics_r.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
diag_r
```

**Reading.**

* **Stability**: the three VARs are stable (largest root `r fmt(max(diag_r$max_root))` < 1).
* **Adjusted Portmanteau** (H0: no residual autocorrelation): not rejected, p = `r paste(round(diag_r$portmanteau_p, 3), collapse = " / ")`.
* **Multivariate normality** (Jarque-Bera): rejected everywhere (p < 0.001).
* **Multivariate ARCH** (`vars::arch.test`, which Python does not have: Python runs one ARCH-LM per equation): p = `r paste(signif(diag_r$ARCH_mult_p, 3), collapse = " / ")`. Conditional heteroscedasticity is present at system level, which supports Phase 5.

## 2. Granger causality

```{r granger}
# 8 directed pairs x 3 periods, then side by side with Python's p-values.
pairs <- expand.grid(ref = c("BTC", "NVDA"), grp = c("CONVERTS", "PURE"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
gr_r <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(PER), function(n) {
  x <- zoo::coredata(PER[[n]])
  do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(nrow(pairs)), function(i) {
    a <- pairs$ref[i]; b <- pairs$grp[i]
    rbind(data.frame(period = n, cause = a, effect = b, t(granger_pair(x, a, b))),
          data.frame(period = n, cause = b, effect = a, t(granger_pair(x, b, a))))
  }))
}))
py_gr <- read.csv(file.path(RES, "04_granger.csv"), check.names = FALSE)
gcmp <- merge(gr_r, py_gr[, c("period", "cause", "effect", "p_value")], by = c("period", "cause", "effect"), suffixes = c("_R", "_Py"))
write.csv(gcmp, file.path(RES, "04_granger_r_vs_python.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
gcmp[order(gcmp$period, gcmp$cause), ]
```

* **Same conclusion at 5% in both languages** for `r sum((gcmp$p_value_R < 0.05) == (gcmp$p_value_Py < 0.05))` tests out of `r nrow(gcmp)`.
* **Maximum p-value difference**: `r fmt(max(abs(gcmp$p_value_R - gcmp$p_value_Py)))`. It comes from the denominator degrees of freedom: single-equation F test in R, system-wide Wald test in statsmodels.

## 3. Impulse responses (same-day effect)

```{r irf}
# Orthogonalised IRF at h = 0 (Cholesky, same order as Python) for BTC and NVDA shocks on both groups.
irf_r <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(vars_r), function(n) {
  ir <- irf(vars_r[[n]], impulse = c("BTC", "NVDA"), response = c("CONVERTS", "PURE"), n.ahead = 10, ortho = TRUE, boot = FALSE)$irf
  do.call(rbind, lapply(names(ir), function(s) data.frame(period = n, shock = s, response = c("CONVERTS", "PURE"), irf_h0 = ir[[s]][1, ])))
}))
py_irf <- read.csv(file.path(RES, "04_irf.csv"), check.names = FALSE)
py_irf <- py_irf[py_irf$h == 0, ]
icmp <- merge(irf_r, py_irf[, c("period", "shock", "response", "irf")], by = c("period", "shock", "response"))
icmp$reldiff <- abs(icmp$irf_h0 / icmp$irf - 1)
write.csv(icmp, file.path(RES, "04_irf_r_vs_python.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
icmp
```

Maximum relative difference on the same-day effect: `r fmt(max(icmp$reldiff))`. In R, the response of CONVERTS to an NVDA shock goes from `r round(irf_r$irf_h0[irf_r$period == "pre-pivot" & irf_r$shock == "NVDA" & irf_r$response == "CONVERTS"], 4)` before the pivot to `r round(irf_r$irf_h0[irf_r$period == "post-pivot" & irf_r$shock == "NVDA" & irf_r$response == "CONVERTS"], 4)` after, as in Python.

## 4. Cointegration (Johansen and Engle-Granger)

```{r coint}
# Same pairs, periods and lag choice (k_ar_diff read from Python's table) so only the software differs.
py_c <- read.csv(file.path(RES, "04_cointegration.csv"), check.names = FALSE)
PAIRS <- list(c("CONVERTS", "BTC"), c("PURE", "BTC"), c("CONVERTS", "NVDA"), c("PURE", "NVDA"))
co_r <- do.call(rbind, lapply(PAIRS, function(pr) do.call(rbind, lapply(names(LPER), function(n) {
  y <- zoo::coredata(LPER[[n]][, pr]); lab <- paste0(pr[1], "–", pr[2])
  k <- py_c$k_ar_diff[py_c$pair == lab & py_c$period == n]
  cbind(data.frame(pair = lab, period = n, k_ar_diff = k), johansen_pair(y, k), EG_stat = eg_stat(y[, 1], y[, 2]))
}))))
ccmp <- merge(co_r, py_c[, c("pair", "period", "trace_r0", "maxeig_r0", "rank_trace", "EG_stat", "EG_p")],
              by = c("pair", "period"), suffixes = c("_R", "_Py"))
write.csv(ccmp, file.path(RES, "04_cointegration_r_vs_python.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
ccmp[, c("pair", "period", "trace_r0_R", "trace_r0_Py", "cv95_trace_r0", "rank_trace_R", "rank_trace_Py",
         "maxeig_r0_R", "maxeig_r0_Py", "rank_maxeig", "EG_stat_R", "EG_stat_Py", "EG_p")]
```

**Comparison.**

* **Trace statistics.** Maximum R / Python difference: `r fmt(max(abs(ccmp$trace_r0_R - ccmp$trace_r0_Py)))`.
* **Critical values.** They differ clearly. For r = 0 at the 5% level, urca gives `r round(co_r$cv95_trace_r0[1], 2)` and statsmodels `r round(py_c$cv95_trace_r0[1], 2)`: the two packages do not use the same table of critical values for this model (unrestricted constant).
* **Ranks.** They coincide in `r sum(ccmp$rank_trace_R == ccmp$rank_trace_Py)` cases out of `r nrow(ccmp)`. The only pair where the two languages differ is **CONVERTS–NVDA**, on the full sample and before the pivot. The trace statistic is identical there (`r round(ccmp$trace_r0_R[ccmp$pair == "CONVERTS–NVDA" & ccmp$period == "full"], 2)`), but it exceeds the statsmodels critical value and not the urca one. The maximum eigenvalue test, on the other hand, rejects r = 0 in both languages (rank_maxeig = `r paste(co_r$rank_maxeig[co_r$pair == "CONVERTS–NVDA" & co_r$period != "post-pivot"], collapse = " / ")` in R). **The CONVERTS–NVDA cointegration is therefore borderline**: it depends on the test and on the table of critical values used. This point is carried into the conclusions.
* **Engle-Granger.** The ADF statistic on the residuals differs by at most `r fmt(max(abs(ccmp$EG_stat_R - ccmp$EG_stat_Py)))`, because the number of lags chosen by AIC is not exactly the same in ur.df and in statsmodels. The MacKinnon p-value computed by Python remains the reference.

## 5. VECM

```{r vecm}
# VECM (cajorls, r = 1) on the pairs where PYTHON's trace test finds rank 1 (so parameters can be compared even if urca's tables are stricter).
vecm_r <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(nrow(co_r)), function(i) {
  if (ccmp$rank_trace_Py[ccmp$pair == co_r$pair[i] & ccmp$period == co_r$period[i]] < 1) return(NULL)
  pr <- strsplit(co_r$pair[i], "–")[[1]]; n <- co_r$period[i]
  y <- zoo::coredata(LPER[[n]][, pr])
  cj <- ca.jo(y, type = "trace", ecdet = "none", K = co_r$k_ar_diff[i] + 1, spec = "transitory")
  cr <- cajorls(cj, r = 1)
  a <- coef(cr$rlm)["ect1", ]
  data.frame(pair = co_r$pair[i], period = n, beta_reference = cr$beta[2, 1],
             alpha_group = a[1], alpha_reference = a[2], half_life_group = half_life(a[1]))
}))
py_v <- read.csv(file.path(RES, "04_vecm.csv"), check.names = FALSE)
vcmp <- merge(vecm_r[, c("pair", "period", "beta_reference", "alpha_group", "half_life_group")],
              py_v[, c("pair", "period", "beta_reference", "alpha_group", "half-life group (d)")],
              by = c("pair", "period"), suffixes = c("_R", "_Py"))
write.csv(vcmp, file.path(RES, "04_vecm_r_vs_python.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
vcmp
```

The two languages give the same cointegrating vector and the same adjustment coefficients:

* maximum difference on β = `r fmt(max(abs(vcmp$beta_reference_R - vcmp$beta_reference_Py)))`;
* maximum difference on the group's α = `r fmt(max(abs(vcmp$alpha_group_R - vcmp$alpha_group_Py)))`;
* half-lives (in trading days): `r paste(round(vcmp$half_life_group, 1), collapse = " / ")` in R, vs `r paste(round(vcmp[["half-life group (d)"]], 1), collapse = " / ")` in Python.

## Conclusion of the comparison

R (`vars`, `urca`) and Python (`statsmodels`) reach the **same conclusions** on:

* the VAR order;
* the significant Granger tests;
* the same-day effects;
* the Johansen ranks, **except for CONVERTS–NVDA**, whose cointegration (full sample and pre-pivot) is borderline: kept by statsmodels and by the maximum eigenvalue test, rejected by the trace test with urca's table;
* the VECM parameters.

The differences have two identified causes: the form of the Granger test (F on one equation vs Wald on the system), which changes no conclusion, and the Johansen critical-value tables, which change the conclusion for CONVERTS–NVDA.
